site.title: dukecodes DevSecOps Roadmap
headline: From zero to job-ready.
Every claim has proof.
lede: Ten milestones on a homelab I'm building myself, from network segmentation to Kubernetes and cloud security. Each one ends with proof you can check: scans, failing-then-passing tests, blocked attacks, and explainers in plain English. No tech background assumed.
footer: . Design: Mission Control, shared by every dukecodes repo.

doneWhen: every row has a score from 0 to 3

milestones.title: Foundations
build: Mission Control → Start here: reality check · Before you start · Rack & power
proof: repo with a threat model, two decision records and a secret-scanning gate that provably blocks a planted key
plain: t
Set up one safe way to manage everything, write down what you are protecting and from whom, and make your code repository refuse secrets.
why: t

Every later control rests on two things: an admin identity an attacker can't borrow, and a written model of what you defend and from whom. Without the model, security work is guesswork. Without signed, scanned commits, the repository that will hold your whole infrastructure becomes the easiest way in.

milestones.title: Segmentation
build: Mission Control → Network edge · Learning lab (the DevSec lab behind OPNsense)
proof: A network diagram and zone matrix in git, plus scan and packet-capture evidence that the DevSec lab cannot reach the home network
careful: Scan only from the lab, and only toward networks you own.
plain: t
Split the network into zones so a hacked device can only reach what it is allowed to, then prove it by attacking yourself.
why: t

A flat network lets one compromised device talk to everything. Segmentation shrinks the blast radius: a hacked smart plug or a lab VM should reach only what a rule explicitly allows. A diagram is a claim; a failed connection attempt from the attacker's side is the proof.
story: "How would you segment a network, and how do you know it works?" Zones with default deny, each allowed flow justified, then proof from the attacker's side: nmap from the lab, the dropped packets in a capture, and the IPv6 route you remembered to test.

doneWhen: default is deny and every allowed flow has a one-line reason

doneWhen: a lab VM gets an address from the lab range and nothing else

doneWhen: gitleaks finds nothing and no password or Wi-Fi key appears in the files

milestones.title: Hardened hosts
build: Mission Control → Prepare the mini PCs · Install Proxmox · Secure the nodes
proof: An Ansible role that hardens all five nodes, runs cleanly twice in a row, and a Lynis score before and after
careful: Change one node first, with a keyboard and screen attached. A bad SSH change can lock you out.
plain: t
Lock down every server the same way using code, and measure how much safer it got.
why: t

Servers are where attackers land. Hardening by hand drifts: five machines end up with five slightly different settings, and nobody remembers why. Hardening as code is repeatable and reviewable, and a before-and-after audit turns "I hardened it" into a number someone else can check.
story: "How do you harden Linux servers at scale?" One role in git, a check-mode dry run first, idempotence as the test, and Lynis numbers before and after, with every remaining warning explained.

milestones.title: Infrastructure as code
build: Mission Control → Services (the Debian 13 VM template)
proof: A Terraform module that builds a Debian 13 VM on Proxmox, a CI scan that fails on a planted misconfiguration, and a full rebuild from git
plain: t
Create servers from code instead of clicking, so every change can be reviewed and scanned before it happens.
why: t

Infrastructure made by clicking can't be reviewed, diffed or rebuilt. Once it is code, every change goes through the same pull request, scan and review as application code. That is where security scanning gets its leverage: a misconfiguration is caught as a failed check instead of found in production.
story: "How do you keep infrastructure changes safe?" Code review plus automated policy: a planted open-firewall rule failed CI before it reached a server, the token can touch one pool only, and the VM rebuilds from git in minutes.

milestones.title: Identity & secrets
build: Mission Control → Remote access · Learning lab
proof: A Tailscale access policy in git with tests that run on every pull request, and secrets that only exist in git as ciphertext
plain: t
Control who can reach what by identity rather than by network location, and keep passwords and keys encrypted everywhere.
why: t

Most breaches use valid credentials. Access based on identity (which person, on which device, to which port) beats access based on network location. Secrets are credentials at rest: if one exists in plaintext anywhere it can be copied, it will eventually leak.
story: "How do you manage access and secrets?" Access policy as code with tests, so a too-wide grant fails review; secrets encrypted in git, inventoried, and one rotated end to end as proof the process works.

text: Put the tailnet policy in git so it matches the live policy (after you decide the three pending changes)
doneWhen: the file in git and the live policy are identical

text: Add tests to the policy: cases that must be allowed and cases that must be denied
doneWhen: widening a grant makes a test fail

text: Run the policy through CI: test on pull requests, apply on main, using an OAuth client scoped to the policy only and stored as a GitHub secret
doneWhen: a merged pull request shows up in Tailscale's configuration log

text: Encrypt one real secret file with SOPS and age
doneWhen: git holds only ciphertext and your age key is backed up offline

text: Write a secrets inventory with names only, never values
doneWhen: each secret lists where it lives, who can read it and how to rotate it

text: Rotate one secret end to end
doneWhen: the old value is revoked and proven dead

milestones.title: Detection
build: Mission Control → Monitoring & power · Phase 2: OPNsense router + VLANs
proof: A Suricata alert for your own M1 scan, visible in Grafana, a custom detection you triggered on purpose, and an incident write-up
plain: t
Collect logs in one place, get alerted when something suspicious happens, and prove the alert fires by setting it off yourself.
why: t

Prevention fails eventually; detection is how you find out. An alert you have never seen fire is a hope, not a control. The test is simple: cause the bad thing on purpose and check the alert arrives where you will see it.
story: "Tell me about a detection you built." The scan you ran in M1, caught by Suricata, visible in Grafana within seconds; the custom SSH alert you fired on purpose; and the week of tuning that cut the noise.

doneWhen: rules load and a test alert appears
the alert in Grafana matches the scan's timestamp

doneWhen: you trigger it on purpose and it reaches your phone or inbox
every suppressed alert has a written reason

milestones.title: Secure pipeline
build: Mission Control → Learning lab (Git hosting and CI with Forgejo on dev)
proof: A pipeline that blocks a pull request adding a known-vulnerable dependency, and a container image that is signed and ships with an SBOM anyone can verify
plain: t
Make the build system check your code and its ingredients for known problems on every change, and stamp what it produces so nobody can swap it later.
why: t

Attackers increasingly skip your code and go after the build: a poisoned dependency, a leaked CI token, an image swapped after it was tested. A secure pipeline checks code, dependencies and configuration on every change, runs with as little access as possible, and signs what it builds so anyone can check where it came from.
story: "How do you secure a CI/CD pipeline?" A gate that blocked a real CVE before merge, images signed at build and verified at deploy, an SBOM for every build, and the pipeline's own attack surface (runner isolation, pinned actions, scoped tokens) reviewed like application code.

doneWhen: the app runs locally and you can name the CVE and what it allows

doneWhen: an ADR says what a malicious job on that runner could still reach

text: Add gates that fail the build on high findings: Semgrep for code, Trivy for dependencies and the image, gitleaks for secrets
doneWhen: the planted CVE fails the pipeline and the upgrade makes it pass

text: Generate an SBOM with Syft for every image
doneWhen: you can answer "do we ship library X, and which version?" from the SBOM alone

text: Sign the image with cosign and verify the signature before every deploy
doneWhen: an unsigned or modified image is refused

text: Harden the pipeline itself: actions pinned by commit SHA, tokens with the least access, zizmor on the workflow files
doneWhen: zizmor reports nothing you have not explained in writing

text: Mirror the app to a public GitHub repo with the same gates
doneWhen: its README shows the passing pipeline and links the SBOM

text: Add an OWASP ZAP baseline scan of the running app to the pipeline
doneWhen: a missing security header fails the scan and adding it makes the scan pass

Change one byte of the image after signing and run the verification. It must fail.
From a fork, open a pull request that edits the workflow. Your secrets must not be available to it.

milestones.title: Kubernetes security
build: Mission Control → Learning lab (Kubernetes with k3s on dev)
proof: A kube-bench report before and after hardening, admission policies that reject a privileged pod, and a Falco alert for a shell opened inside a container
plain: t
Run containers on a small Kubernetes cluster, set rules that refuse unsafe ones, and get an alert when someone opens a shell inside one.
why: t

Kubernetes runs many workloads on shared machines, so one badly configured pod can become a foothold on the node underneath. Security comes in layers: who may call the API (RBAC), what a pod may ask for (admission policy), which pods may talk to each other (network policy), and what to watch while it runs (runtime detection). Each layer assumes the one before it can fail.
story: "How would you secure a Kubernetes cluster?" Layers, each with proof: kube-bench numbers before and after, a privileged pod refused by policy, a default-deny network tested from inside the cluster, and a Falco alert for a shell you opened yourself.

doneWhen: shows Ready and you can explain what each control-plane part does

text: Run kube-bench and save the report
doneWhen: and you have picked the five findings to fix first

doneWhen: proves the account cannot read Secrets outside its namespace

tags, only images you signed in M6
doneWhen: each bad pod is rejected with a clear message

text: Add a default-deny NetworkPolicy, then allow only the flows each app needs
doneWhen: a test pod proves a blocked connection really fails

doneWhen: into a pod raises an alert you can see in Grafana
a before/after table explains every remaining finding

breakIt: Try to deploy a privileged pod, a pod that mounts the host's filesystem, and a pod with an unsigned image. All three must be rejected.
Check that the cluster's network plugin enforces NetworkPolicy before you rely on it. A policy that is accepted but not enforced is worse than none, because you think you are protected.

milestones.title: Resilience & IR
proof: A timed restore drill measured against written targets, an incident runbook, and a postmortem of an attack you simulated in the lab
careful: Run attack simulations only on lab VMs you own, never on the home network.
plain: t
Prove you can get everything back after a disaster, and practise what to do if you get hacked, before it happens for real.
why: t

A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a control. Ransomware goes after backups first, so two questions matter: can an attacker on one machine delete the backups, and how long does a full recovery really take? Incident response works the same way: under stress you do what you have practised, so you practise.
story: "Tell me about a time something went wrong." A restore drill with measured times against written targets, what you found when you checked whether the backup credential could delete backups, and a postmortem of a simulated attack mapped to ATT&CK.

text: Write an RPO/RTO table for each service: how much data you can afford to lose and how long it can be down
doneWhen: every target has a reason, not only a number

text: Restore a VM from Proxmox Backup Server onto a different node and time it
doneWhen: the measured time sits in the ledger next to its target

text: Restore from the second copy (the USB disk or the offsite copy) with the main backup server switched off
Check whether the backup credential on a node can delete or overwrite backups
doneWhen: an ADR records the answer and, if yes, the fix

text: Write an incident runbook from the Maintenance & incidents chapter: detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn
doneWhen: someone else could follow it from page one

text: Run one Atomic Red Team test in the DevSec lab, then write a blameless postmortem with
doneWhen: it says whether M5 detected the test, how fast, and what you changed

breakIt: Tabletop: a node shows signs of compromise at 2 a.m. Walk the runbook out loud and time each decision.
Delete a test file, then restore it from last night's backup. How far back could you really go?

milestones.title: Cloud mirror
build: Beyond Mission Control (an AWS account you create)
proof: A Terraform baseline for a new AWS account, a Prowler report before and after, and the M6 app deployed through a GitHub OIDC role with no stored keys
cert: AWS Solutions Architect – Associate (AWS Security – Specialty later)
careful: Cloud costs real money. Set the budget alarm before anything else, and tear everything down when you finish.
plain: t
Rebuild the same security habits in the cloud, where most of these jobs are, and prove the account is locked down with a scanner.
why: t

Most DevSecOps jobs run on a cloud provider. The ideas carry over from the lab (identity, segmentation, logging, least privilege), but the shared responsibility model moves the line: the provider secures the hardware and the platform, you secure everything you configure. Most cloud breaches are configuration mistakes, so you prove the configuration.
story: "How would you secure a new AWS account?" A Terraform baseline applied from CI, Prowler numbers before and after, a deploy role only your main branch can assume, and a bill that proves you cleaned up.

text: Create an AWS account and lock the root user: MFA on, no access keys, a budget alarm set low
doneWhen: root is for emergencies only and the alarm has emailed you once as a test

text: Set up IAM Identity Center for your daily login
doneWhen: day-to-day work uses neither root nor a long-lived access key

text: Write Terraform for the baseline in
: CloudTrail in every region, account-level S3 Block Public Access, and a GitHub OIDC role for deploys
doneWhen: is clean and CI applies it

doneWhen: a before/after table explains every remaining high finding

doneWhen: the pipeline runs with no AWS keys stored anywhere

def: Three copies of your data, on two kinds of storage, with one copy somewhere else. Today, one copy should also be offline or unchangeable, so ransomware can't reach it.
Microsoft's directory for Windows networks. It holds users, computers and groups, checks who is logging on, and pushes settings to every joined machine.
A Kubernetes gatekeeper that checks every request to create something and can refuse it, for example a container asking for too much power.
Architecture decision record. A one-page note on a choice you made, the options you weighed and why you picked one.

A password-like key that lets a program, not a person, use a service. Give each tool its own, with only the access it needs.
A library of small, safe tests that mimic real attacker techniques, used to check whether your detections fire.

How much damage one compromised device or account can do. Segmentation and least privilege shrink it.
A separate line of work in git. You merge it into main when it's ready.

The AWS service that records who did what in your account. The cloud's security camera.
A saved snapshot of changes in git, with a message saying why.
Adding a cryptographic signature to a commit so others can check it really came from you and wasn't changed.
Rules in Entra ID that decide whether a sign-in is allowed, based on who, which device, from where, and whether MFA was used.
A packaged app with everything it needs to run, isolated from other apps but sharing the host's operating system kernel.
A tool that signs container images and checks those signatures before they run.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. A public ID for a known security bug, such as CVE-2026-33634.
Dynamic application security testing. Attacking a running app from the outside to find weaknesses.
A rule style where everything is blocked unless a rule explicitly allows it.
Several independent layers of protection, so one failure doesn't mean a breach.
A rule that turns a suspicious event in your logs into an alert someone sees.
DomainKeys Identified Mail. A signature a sending mail server adds, so the receiver can check the message really came from that domain and wasn't changed.
A domain's published rule for what receivers should do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM checks: deliver it, quarantine it or reject it.
The internet's phone book. It turns names like example.com into addresses computers can use.
When the real system no longer matches what your code or documents say it should be.
Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure AD. It signs people in to Microsoft 365 and other apps and enforces Conditional Access.
: one row per proof, with the claim, where the evidence is, and how to check it again.
A tool that watches what containers do while they run and alerts on suspicious behaviour, such as a shell opening inside one.
A device or program that decides which network traffic is allowed through, based on rules.
Self-hosted software for git repositories and CI, like a small GitHub you run yourself.
A scanner that searches files and git history for passwords, keys and tokens.
A dashboard tool that turns metrics and logs into charts and alerts.
Settings in Active Directory, grouped into GPOs, that every matching user or computer in the domain must follow, such as password rules.
Removing what a system doesn't need and locking down what's left, so there's less to attack.
Infrastructure as code. Describing servers and networks in text files, so changes can be reviewed, tested and repeated.
Identity and access management. Who can do what, on which resource.
Safe to run again. A second run changes nothing because everything is already as described.
Intrusion detection system. Watches network traffic and raises an alert on known attack patterns.
The practised steps for handling a security problem: detect, contain, remove the cause, recover, learn.
Microsoft's cloud service for managing laptops and phones: it enrols devices, checks they meet a compliance policy and pushes settings to them.
Indicator of compromise. A clue that something bad happened, such as a known-bad domain, file hash or sender address.
Intrusion prevention system. An IDS that also blocks the traffic it flags.
A small, easy-to-install version of Kubernetes, good for labs and small servers.
A tool that checks a Kubernetes cluster against the CIS security benchmark and lists what to fix.
A system that runs many containers across many machines, restarts them when they fail and controls how they talk.
A Kubernetes admission controller where you write rules such as "no privileged pods" in plain YAML.
Give each person and program only the access its job needs, nothing more.
A tool that audits a Linux server's security settings and gives it a hardening score.
Multi-factor authentication. Proving who you are with two things, such as a password and a code from your phone.
A named area inside Kubernetes that keeps one app's resources apart from another's.
A Kubernetes rule that says which pods may talk to which.
A network scanner that finds which devices are on a network and which ports they have open.
OpenID Connect. A standard way for one system to vouch for an identity to another, so a CI job can get cloud access without a stored password.
Free, open-source firewall and router software.
Recording the raw network traffic on a link so you can inspect exactly what was sent.
A message that pretends to be someone trusted, to trick you into clicking a link, opening a file or handing over a password.
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network address.
A written review after an incident: what happened, why, and what changes. Blameless means it fixes systems, not people.
A check that runs on your own computer before git saves a commit.
A scanner that checks a cloud account against security best practices and lists what's wrong.
Free software that turns a computer into a host for many virtual machines and containers.
Proxmox's backup software. It stores encrypted, deduplicated backups of virtual machines.
A request to merge a branch. It's where checks run and reviews happen.
Role-based access control. Permissions are given to roles, and people or programs are given roles.
A project folder with its full change history, stored by git. Often called a repo.
Recovery point objective. How much data you can afford to lose, measured as time since the last good backup.
Recovery time objective. How long a service can be down before it's restored.
An AWS setting that stops storage buckets from being made public, even by mistake.
Static application security testing. Reading source code for security bugs without running it.
Software bill of materials. A list of every component and version inside a piece of software.
Software composition analysis. Checking the libraries your code uses for known vulnerabilities.
Anything that grants access: a password, an API token, a private key.
Searching files and history for secrets before they leak, or right after.
Splitting a network into zones, so a problem in one zone can't spread freely to the others.
Referring to a tool by its exact fingerprint instead of a version name, so nobody can swap it under a familiar label.
The cloud split: the provider secures the hardware and platform, you secure what you configure on it.
Security information and event management. A system that collects logs from everywhere and searches them for signs of attack.
A tool that encrypts the values in configuration files, so secrets can live in git as unreadable ciphertext.
Sender Policy Framework. A DNS record listing which servers may send mail for a domain.
A widely used SIEM. It collects logs and lets you search them and alert on them with its query language, SPL.
Secure Shell. An encrypted way to log in to and control a remote computer.
A firewall that remembers connections, so replies to traffic you started get back in while unsolicited traffic is blocked.
A checklist of six threat types: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.
A range of network addresses that sit together, like the house numbers on one street.
Breaking in through a tool, library or service you trust instead of attacking your own code.
An open-source IDS and IPS that inspects network traffic against rules.
A tool that generates an SBOM for a container image or a folder.
Talking through an incident scenario step by step, without touching real systems, to find gaps in your plan.
A service that builds a private, encrypted network between your devices using WireGuard, without opening ports on your router.
A command-line tool for packet capture.
An IaC tool that creates and changes infrastructure from text files and shows a plan before it acts.
Terraform's record of what it built. It can contain secrets, so it must be protected.
A written answer to four questions: what are we protecting, from whom, what can go wrong, and what are we doing about it.
A scanner for known vulnerabilities, secrets and misconfigurations in code, containers and IaC.
A line where data or control passes between parts you trust differently, such as the internet and your network. Threats cluster there.
Virtual LAN. A way to split one physical network into separate virtual networks.
Virtual machine. A whole computer simulated in software, running on a host.
A fast, modern VPN protocol that connects devices with key pairs.
OWASP ZAP, a free DAST scanner. It attacks a running web app from the outside and reports weaknesses such as missing security headers.
Never trust a connection because of where it comes from. Check identity and device on every request.
A scanner that finds security problems in GitHub Actions workflow files.

scenarios.title: Log real proof
summary: Tick a rep, add its ledger row and the evidence file.
scenarios.cmd: git commit -am "M1-R4: nmap from the lab, home unreachable"
lesson: Every gate passed, so the page rebuilds on merge with the new proof linked. That's the only way progress shows up here.

scenarios.title: Tick a rep with no proof
scenarios.finding: M2-R4 is ticked but has no ledger row
lesson: Claims without evidence never reach the page. Add the proof to

scenarios.title: Publish a real address
summary: Paste raw scan output with private IPs in it.
scenarios.cmd: git add evidence/m1-nmap.txt && git commit -m "scan output"
lesson: Real addresses and hostnames hand an attacker a map of the network.
swaps them for documentation examples such as 192.0.2.10.

scenarios.title: Commit a key by mistake
summary: An API token sneaks into a notes file.
lesson: Caught on the laptop before it left. A leaked key gets revoked, not only deleted: git keeps every old version.

scenarios.title: Skip the hooks
lesson: Local hooks are a convenience; CI is the gate. Two layers means one bypass isn't a breach. That's defense in depth.

scenarios.title: Pin an action to a tag
summary: Use actions/checkout@v7 instead of a commit SHA.
scenarios.finding: unpinned-uses: actions/checkout@v7 is not pinned to a SHA
lesson: A tag can be moved to point at malicious code, as happened to
in March 2026. A full commit SHA can't move.
